Loading Data

```{r}
cer <- read.csv("cereals.csv")
```

Three of the 77 cereals have missing values (one in carbo, one in sugars, two in potass), so 74 remain. I clustered on the 13 numeric variables (calories through rating), excluding name, mfr and type, after standardizing them with scale()

```{r}
cat("Rows before:", nrow(cer), "\n")
print(colSums(is.na(cer)))
# cereals have placeholder -1 for missing in the original dataset? check
print(sapply(cer[,4:16], function(x) sum(x < 0)))
cer <- na.omit(cer)
cat("Rows after na.omit:", nrow(cer), "\n")
rownames(cer) <- cer$name
num <- cer[, 4:16]            # drop name, mfr, type
num <- num[, sapply(num, is.numeric)]
print(names(num))
z <- scale(num)
d <- dist(z, method = "euclidean")
```

```{r}
# Agnes: agglomerative coefficient
meths <- c("single","complete","average", "ward")
ac <- sapply(meths, function(m) agnes(z, method = m)$ac)
print(round(ac, 4))
```

Ward Linkage is the best method. It has the highest coefficient, meaning the strongest clustering structure. Single linkage is the worst because it chains observations together.

```{r}
best <- "ward"
ag <- agnes(z, method = best)
pltree(ag, cex = 0.5, hang = -1, main = "Agnes - Ward (normalized data)")
rect.hclust(as.hclust(ag), k = 4, border = 2:5)
```

```{r}
hc <- as.hclust(ag)
# Heights of last merges and silhouette for k
print(round(tail(hc$height, 10), 2))
for (k in 2:8) {
  cl <- cutree(hc, k)
  cat("k =", k, " avg silhouette =", round(mean(silhouette(cl, d)[, 3]), 4), " sizes:", table(cl), "\n")
}
cer <- na.omit(cer)
rownames(cer) <- cer$name
num <- cer[, 4:16]
z <- scale(num)
hc <- as.hclust(agnes(z, method="ward"))
K <- 4
cl <- cutree(hc, K)
cat("\n== Cluster means (original units) ==\n")
print(round(aggregate(num, list(cluster=cl), mean)[,-1] |> cbind(n=as.vector(table(cl))), 2))
cat("\n== Members ==\n")
for (k in 1:K) cat("Cluster", k, ":", paste(rownames(num)[cl==k], collapse=", "), "\n")
cat("\nMfr by cluster:\n"); print(table(cl, cer$mfr))
```

```{r}
assign_centroid <- function(newz, cent) apply(newz, 1, function(r) which.min(colSums((t(cent)-r)^2)))
stab <- function(seed, frac=0.5) {
  set.seed(seed)
  idx <- sample(nrow(z), round(nrow(z)*frac))
  A <- z[idx,,drop=FALSE]; B <- z[-idx,,drop=FALSE]
  clA <- cutree(hclust(dist(A), "ward.D2"), K)
  cent <- apply(A, 2, function(c) tapply(c, clA, mean))
  predB <- assign_centroid(B, cent)
  # map to full-data clusters: compare with full cluster labels via best matching (centroids of A vs full-data centroids)
  fullB <- cl[-idx]
  # Align A's clusters to full clusters via the full-data labels of A's members (majority)
  map <- sapply(1:K, function(k) { t <- table(factor(cl[idx][clA==k], levels=1:K)); which.max(t) })
  mean(map[predB] == fullB)
}
cat("\n== Stability: 50/50 split, single seed ==\n"); print(stab(1))
res <- sapply(1:200, stab)
cat("Mean agreement over 200 random splits:", round(mean(res),3), " range:", round(range(res),3), "\n")
cat("Same at k=2..6 (mean of 100 splits):\n")
for (kk in 2:6) { K <- kk; cl <- cutree(hc, K); cat(" k=",kk," ", round(mean(sapply(1:100, stab)),3), "\n") }
K <- 4; cl <- cutree(hc, K)
```

Q) How many clusters would I choose?

Ans) k=4 gives clusters that are easy to interpret and reasonably stable

Comment on Structure and Stability

Structure: Cluster 1 is a tiny outlier group, and clusters 3 and 4 are the largest and most natural groups. Manufacturers do not separate cleanly, since every cluster except 1 mixes General Mills, Kellogg’s, Post and others. Clusters follow nutrition, and the consumer ratings line up with it (sugary cereals rate lowest, bran cereals highest).
Stability test: I split the data 50/50 at random, ran Ward on partition A, assigned each record in B to the nearest A-centroid, and compared with the full-data clusters. Over 200 random splits the mean agreement was 78.7%, with a range of 38% to 100%. A single split (seed 1) gave 81%.
Stability across k: Agreement was 76% at k=2, 67% at k=3, 79% at k=4, 78% at k=5 and 73% at k=6. So k=4 is among the most stable choices.
Verdict: The clusters are moderately stable, not very stable. The three-member bran cluster and the boundary between clusters 2 and 4 cause most of the disagreement, so I would not treat individual assignments as firm.




Rand-type check using flexible approach on seed 1 with Adjusted rand

```{r}


#Healthy cereals 

vars <- c("calories","protein","fat","sodium","fiber","carbo","sugars","potass","vitamins")
x <- cer[, vars]
cat("SDs raw:\n"); print(round(apply(x,2,sd),2))
for (mode in c("raw","scaled")) {
  m <- if (mode=="raw") x else scale(x)
  ag <- agnes(m, method="ward"); cat("\n##", mode, " ac =", round(ag$ac,3), "\n")
  for (K in 3:4) {
    cl <- cutree(as.hclust(ag), K)
    cat("K =", K, "\n"); print(round(cbind(aggregate(x, list(cl), mean)[,-1], n=as.vector(table(cl)), rating=aggregate(cer$rating, list(cl), mean)$x),1))
  }
}
ag <- agnes(scale(x), method="ward"); cl <- cutree(as.hclust(ag), 4)
# pick healthy cluster: highest fiber/protein, lowest sugar & calories
cm <- aggregate(x, list(cl), mean)
cat("\nHealthy cluster members (scaled, K=4):\n")
h <- which.min(cm$sugars + cm$calories/10 - cm$fiber*2 - cm$protein*2)
cat("cluster",h,":\n"); print(rownames(x)[cl==h])
cat("Mean rating in that cluster:", mean(cer$rating[cl==h]), "\n")
```

My recommendation is to normalize for the clustering, but to judge “healthy” from raw units.

Why not raw units: The raw units differ wildly. Sodium (SD about 83 mg) and potassium (SD about 71 mg) would dominate protein and fat (SD about 1 g). On raw data the clusters are mostly “low-sodium vs high-sodium” groups.
Choose variables on purpose: Use only the nutrition variables: calories, protein, fat, sodium, fiber, carbo, sugars, potass and vitamins. Drop shelf, weight and cups, which are not about health. Also drop rating, which is an outcome, not a nutrient.
Judge on absolute levels: Z-scores are relative to this sample, and a cereal can be below average and still unhealthy. So read the cluster means in original units against absolute criteria such as low sugar and sodium and higher fiber and protein.

With standardized nutrition variables and Ward at k=4, the results are:

Cluster	and	Notes
Cluster 1: 3 Observations |	Highest fiber and protein (the three bran cereals), but sodium is 177 mg
Cluster 2: 39 Observations | High sugar (10.3 g) and calories (116)
Cluster 3: 23 Observations |	Sodium of 226 mg, highest vitamins
Cluster 4: 9 Observations |	Calories 82, sugars 2.3 g, fat 0.1 g, sodium about 2 mg, rating 63

The best school choice is cluster 4, which includes Puffed Rice, Puffed Wheat, the Shredded Wheat varieties, Maypo, Frosted Mini-Wheats, Raisin Squares and Strawberry Fruit Wheats. It has very low sodium and fat and little sugar, though fiber is only moderate (about 2 g). 

Two cautions:

Frosted Mini-Wheats (7 g sugar) and Raisin Squares (6 g) are the weakest members of cluster 4 on sugar.
Cluster membership depends on the variable set. To be sure it matches the schools’ goals, we could add hard cutoffs, for example sugars of 6 g or less and sodium of 150 mg or less, on top of the cluster.
